html:
The farm policy of the European Economic Community, now the European Union, launched in 1962. It pays subsidies to farmers and for decades took most of the bloc's budget.

The Treaty of Rome called for a common farm policy. Europe remembered wartime hunger, farmers were many and politically strong, especially in France, and governments wanted secure food and steady incomes in the countryside. The CAP guaranteed farmers high prices: the Community bought up what did not sell and taxed cheaper imports.

It worked too well. By the 1970s and 1980s Europe was producing far more than it ate, and the stores of surplus food became known as "butter mountains" and "wine lakes". Surpluses were dumped on world markets. At its height the CAP took around two thirds of the budget.

Reforms from 1992 moved support from prices to direct payments to farmers, and later tied them to the land and to care for the environment instead of output. The CAP still takes about a third of the EU budget and remains a constant source of argument.
sum: The farm policy of the European Economic Community, now the European Union, launched in 1962. It pays subsidies to farmers and for decades took most of the bloc's budget.
